Chapter 6: The Power of Context—How Situations Shape What We Do
Have you ever noticed how sometimes, it’s not really about who you are, but where you are that changes how you act?
The setting—what’s happening around you, even the time of day—can be like a quiet director behind the scenes, nudging your choices in ways that just feel... natural, almost inevitable.
Imagine this: a bunch of coworkers head off to a company retreat. Suddenly, away from their usual office routines, something shifts. People start opening up, sharing stories and ideas they’d never dream of mentioning in a conference room.
Someone who’s usually the quiet type cracks a joke. Another, who hardly ever speaks up, jumps in to lead a game. It’s not that these folks changed overnight—it’s the context that did. And with it, the unwritten rules of how everyone interacts.
It’s so easy to overlook just how much the environment matters. Think about a parent, usually calm and patient at home, suddenly snapping at her kids in the middle of a crowded grocery store. Or a student who seems perfectly confident in a small seminar but freezes up in a huge lecture hall.
Same person, just a different setting—and suddenly, their behavior shifts.
Researchers have uncovered that even tiny changes in context can have a big impact. For example, there’s this story about a group of diners at a restaurant. The menus they get have certain dishes marked as “chef’s specials.” Most people end up ordering those—not because they’re the tastiest, but because those bold highlights catch their eye.
Or take a neighborhood where recycling rates skyrocket after the bins are moved somewhere more visible. The easier it is to do something, the more likely people are to do it.
Here’s the thing—most of us hardly notice these little cues. We like to think our choices are all about our preferences or principles. But often, it’s the situation quietly steering us.
Like that shopper who grabs a candy bar at the checkout, not because she planned to, but because it’s right there, calling her name. Or the commuter who takes a new route to work just because he saw a construction sign, even though the old way never really bothered him before.
Context isn’t just about what we do—it even shifts how we feel.
A quiet park bench gently invites you to reflect, while a bustling café can spark all kinds of conversations. The very same person, dropped into different settings, will think, act, and feel completely differently.
So, what can we do with this?
Well, recognizing the power of context gives us a chance to take back a little control. If we start noticing how our surroundings shape our behavior, we can actually design environments that help us make better choices.
Say a family wants to eat healthier. They might decide to keep a bowl of fresh fruit on the counter instead of a jar of cookies. Or maybe an office wants to encourage more collaboration, so they rearrange the desks to make it easier for people to chat and share ideas.
Most of the time, we’re just moving through life on autopilot, responding to the cues all around us without even realizing it.
But if you pay attention—if you notice the invisible influence of your environment—you can make small changes that lead to big results.
The trick is to spot this silent architect at work... and, whenever you can, use it to your advantage.
